The travellers cross troll country, where the local inhabitants turn out to be slow and stupid in the heat and sharp-witted in the cold, and Cohen is fitted with a set of diamond teeth that solve the greatest inconvenience of his old age. Herrena's band is still on their trail, and the Luggage, separated from its owner and thoroughly bad-tempered about it, crosses the country after them, leaving a trail of people who wish they had not got in its way. With the star now dominating the sky, magic failing across the Disc and the countryside emptying as people head for the cities or for the cults, the party turns toward Ankh-Morpork, where the Octavo and the other seven great spells are kept.

Twoflower is brought close to death and spends the interval in Death's own domain, where he introduces Death and the other Horsemen to a card game they find considerably more absorbing than their duties, which delays them at an awkward moment. The party reaches Ankh-Morpork to find the city in chaos. The red star fills half the sky, ordinary magic barely works, and the streets belong to mobs hunting wizards and to star cults preaching that the light is a deliverance. At Unseen University, Trymon has consolidated his authority and made himself the man who will save the world. Rather than gather the eight orders of wizards to read the spells as tradition requires, he takes the Octavo for himself and reads seven of the great spells directly into his own head, intending to hold all of that power alone. It is more than a human mind can contain. The Things from the Dungeon Dimensions, formless creatures pressing at the edges of reality, take him over and begin using him as a way in, and the Tower of Art at the heart of the University becomes the point where they will break through.

Rincewind climbs the Tower of Art to face what is left of Trymon, is drawn into the nightmare landscape inside his head, and kills him with a half-brick in a sock, driving the Things back out of the world. He then reads the Octavo, and the eighth spell leaves his mind at last; the eight spells spoken together steady the world. The red star proves to be no danger: Great A'Tuin was making for it in order to give birth, and eight small turtles hatch there and swim away carrying eight tiny new worlds, while the Disc passes safely on. Free of the spell for the first time in his life, Rincewind returns to Unseen University to begin learning magic properly. Twoflower, satisfied with his holiday, goes home to the Agatean Empire and leaves the Luggage to Rincewind as a gift. Cohen and Bethan marry, and Cohen accepts a comfortable place among the kingdoms of the Circle Sea.

characters.description: A twelve-year-old boy who has been expelled from a string of schools for trouble he cannot explain, and who struggles with dyslexia and attention problems. Loyal to his mother and fiercely protective of his friends, he is quick-tempered and impulsive but brave. Strange and dangerous things keep happening around him, and he is about to learn why.
characters.name: Percy Jackson

characters.description: Percy's closest friend at Yancy Academy, a nervous boy with a limp and a medical excuse from physical activities who always seems to be watching out for Percy. Easily frightened and quick to make excuses, he is more than he appears and takes his role in Percy's life very seriously.
characters.name: Grover Underwood

characters.description: Percy's devoted mother, who works long hours at low-paying jobs and protects her son with warmth and humor despite an unhappy marriage. She loves the sea and takes Percy to a rented cabin at Montauk beach that holds special meaning for her. She has kept important truths about Percy's father from him to keep him safe.
characters.name: Sally Jackson

characters.description: Percy's crude, selfish stepfather, a heavy gambler who reeks of cigars and beer and treats Percy and Sally with open contempt. Percy privately calls him Smelly Gabe.
characters.name: Gabe Ugliano

characters.description: The immortal centaur who has trained heroes for thousands of years, hidden for a time as Percy's kindly, wheelchair-using Latin teacher Mr. Brunner. As the activities director of Camp Half-Blood, the safe haven for children of the Greek gods, he guides and instructs the young demigods with patience and quiet authority.
characters.name: Chiron

characters.description: The god of wine, sentenced by Zeus to run Camp Half-Blood as punishment and forbidden to drink wine while he serves out his term. Irritable, bored, and dismissive of the campers, he can barely be bothered to remember their names.
characters.name: Dionysus

characters.description: A sharp, strategic demigod with gray eyes and blond hair who has lived at Camp Half-Blood for years and longs to prove herself on a real quest. A daughter of Athena, she is a skilled fighter and planner who tends to Percy when he first arrives, sizing him up at once.
characters.name: Annabeth Chase

characters.description: The friendly, well-liked head counselor of the Hermes cabin, an older camper who welcomes Percy, teaches him swordsmanship, and treats newcomers kindly. He carries a scar across his face and speaks with some bitterness about feeling overlooked by the gods.
characters.name: Luke Castellan

characters.description: A tough, aggressive camper and daughter of Ares, the god of war, who bullies newcomers and takes an immediate dislike to Percy, shoving his head toward a toilet on his first day at camp.
characters.name: Clarisse La Rue

characters.description: The god of the sea and one of the three most powerful gods. During a game he publicly claims Percy as his son, an act that breaks a sworn pact among the greatest gods not to father more children and makes Percy's very existence a source of danger and suspicion. He is a distant father but not an unkind one.
characters.name: Poseidon

characters.description: The god of war, who meets the travelers on their journey in the guise of a swaggering, leather-clad biker. Aggressive and eager for conflict, he strikes a bargain with Percy, offering help and supplies in exchange for a favor.
characters.name: Ares

characters.description: The grim lord of the Underworld and god of the dead, brother of Zeus and Poseidon. Suspected of stealing Zeus's master lightning bolt to start a war among the gods, he is the target Percy's quest leads toward, and he receives Percy in his shadowy palace with fury and his own accusations.
characters.name: Hades

recaps.ending: Percy recovers Zeus's master bolt, defeats the god Ares in single combat using his powers over water, and returns the bolt to Mount Olympus, averting war among the gods; he also forces the return of Hades' stolen helm of darkness. Meeting his father Poseidon face to face, Percy is acknowledged, though the two remain distant. Back at Camp Half-Blood he learns that the entire theft was engineered to set the gods against one another, and that the real thief was Luke Castellan, the counselor who had befriended him, secretly serving the reviving Titan lord Kronos, who seeks to overthrow the gods. Luke tries to kill Percy with a venomous scorpion and then flees to continue serving Kronos. Percy's mother, released from the Underworld, frees herself from her cruel husband Gabe by turning him to stone with Medusa's severed head. Offered the chance to stay at camp year-round, Percy instead decides to live at home and attend school with his mother, keeping a foot in the mortal world. The threat of Kronos and Luke's betrayal remains open for the books to come.
recaps.in_short: Twelve-year-old Percy Jackson discovers that the Greek gods are real and that he is a demigod, the son of the sea god Poseidon. After a monster attack seems to kill his mother, he reaches Camp Half-Blood, a training ground for the gods' children. When Zeus's master lightning bolt is stolen, Percy is blamed, and to prevent a war among the gods he sets out with his friends Annabeth and Grover to find the true thief before the summer solstice. Their journey across the country toward the Underworld's entrance in Los Angeles pits them against monsters and gods, including Ares, who deceives them. In the Underworld Percy learns the bolt has been planted in his own bag and that his mother is held captive; he escapes but must leave her behind. He defeats Ares, returns the bolt to Mount Olympus, and stops the war. He then learns the real thief was his camp friend Luke, secretly serving the reviving Titan lord Kronos. Percy comes home to find his mother freed and chooses to spend the school year in the mortal world.

recaps.text: Twelve-year-old Percy Jackson keeps getting expelled from schools for bizarre incidents he cannot explain. On a class trip to a museum, one of his teachers transforms into a winged monster and attacks him, and afterward everyone insists she never existed and was never his teacher. His anxious friend Grover behaves strangely, and his Latin teacher, Mr. Brunner, seems to know more than he admits. At home Percy is caught between his loving mother, Sally, and his crude, unpleasant stepfather, Gabe. Sensing danger, Sally takes Percy to a seaside cabin, where Grover catches up to them and reveals that monsters are hunting Percy. A bull-headed creature attacks on the road; Percy's mother is seized and vanishes in a flash of gold, and Percy kills the monster before collapsing at the border of a mysterious camp.

Percy wakes at Camp Half-Blood, a hidden haven for the children of the Greek gods, who turn out to be real and still active in the modern world. Mr. Brunner is revealed to be Chiron, an immortal centaur, and the camp is overseen by the sour god Dionysus. Percy meets other young demigods, including the clever Annabeth, the friendly counselor Luke, and the hostile Clarisse, and learns that a camper's godly parent is often unknown. During a game of capture the flag, Percy's power over water surfaces and he is publicly claimed as a son of Poseidon, a forbidden birth under an oath among the most powerful gods. Chiron then reveals that Zeus's master lightning bolt has been stolen and Percy is being blamed; to head off a war among the gods, Percy accepts a quest to recover it, with suspicion pointing toward the Underworld far to the west.

Percy sets out west with Annabeth and Grover toward Los Angeles, where an entrance to the Underworld is said to lie. Vengeful monsters pursue them at every turn: the winged Furies attack aboard a bus, and at a roadside garden statuary shop they narrowly kill Medusa, whose gaze turns victims to stone. At the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Percy is cornered by the fire-breathing Chimera and its mistress; badly hurt, he escapes by plunging into the Mississippi River, where he discovers he can breathe and heal underwater. The travelers press on, low on money and time, racing against a summer-solstice deadline before the gods go to war.

As they continue across the country, the travelers encounter the god Ares, who strikes a bargain with them: in exchange for aid he sends them to retrieve his shield, which leads them into a trap in an abandoned amusement park that they barely escape. They pass through the Lotus Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas, a place where time stands still and guests forget to leave, and only just break free after realizing that days have slipped by and their deadline is closing. Reaching Los Angeles at last, Percy outwits a monster running a waterbed store and finds the hidden entrance to the Underworld.

Percy, Annabeth, and Grover cross the river of the dead and reach the palace of Hades. There Percy discovers, to his horror, that the stolen master bolt has been hidden in his own backpack without his knowledge, and Hades furiously accuses him of also stealing his helm of darkness. Percy finds his captured mother held in the Underworld, but with only three magic escape pearls for four people, he is forced to leave her behind to save his friends and complete the quest. Escaping to a beach, the three are met by the god Ares, who is revealed to have set Percy up and arranged for the bolt to be planted on him. Percy defeats Ares in a duel with his sea powers, forcing him to return Hades' helm, and recovers the master bolt.

Percy flies to New York and climbs to Mount Olympus, returning the master lightning bolt to Zeus and averting war among the gods. He meets his father, Poseidon, who acknowledges him though the two remain distant. Back at Camp Half-Blood, Percy learns the deeper truth: the theft was meant to turn the gods against each other, and the real thief was Luke, the friendly counselor, secretly working for the reviving Titan lord Kronos, who wants to destroy the gods. Luke tries to kill Percy with a venomous scorpion before escaping to serve Kronos. At home, Percy finds his mother alive and freed from her cruel husband Gabe, whom she has turned to stone with Medusa's head. Given the choice to live at camp year-round, Percy decides to spend the school year at home with his mother, knowing that greater dangers, and Kronos, still lie ahead.

characters.description: The youngest of four siblings sent to stay in the country house of an old Professor while the war goes on. Curious and honest, she is the first to step through the back of a large wardrobe and find herself in a snow-covered land where it is always winter. Warm-hearted and quietly brave, she befriends a faun there and comes home certain the other world is real, even when the others refuse to believe her.
characters.name: Lucy Pevensie

characters.description: The second-youngest Pevensie, sharp-tongued and easily sulky, often quarreling with his siblings. Following Lucy into the wardrobe, he meets a tall, imperious woman who calls herself the Queen of Narnia. She feeds him an enchanted sweet, Turkish Delight, that leaves him craving more and eager to please her, and she coaxes out of him news of his brother and sisters. Flattered and greedy, he begins to keep secrets from the others.
characters.name: Edmund Pevensie

characters.description: The eldest of the four children, responsible and level-headed, who tries to look after his younger siblings and keep the peace among them. He is fair-minded and reluctant to believe fantastic stories without proof.
characters.name: Peter Pevensie

characters.description: The elder sister, sensible and cautious, inclined to worry and to act as a second mother to the younger two. She prefers practical comfort and is slow to accept anything strange or dangerous.
characters.name: Susan Pevensie

characters.description: A faun, half man and half goat, whom Lucy meets by a lamp-post in the snowy Narnian woods. He carries parcels and an umbrella and invites her to tea in his cave, where he is kindly and musical. But he serves the ruler who has cursed the land, and he has been ordered to hand over any human he finds. Ashamed, he cannot go through with betraying Lucy and instead helps her return safely.
characters.name: Mr. Tumnus

characters.description: A tall, proud, unnaturally pale woman who has seized power over Narnia and holds it under an enchantment of endless winter in which Christmas never comes. She rides a sledge drawn by reindeer and carries a wand that can turn living creatures to stone. Cruel and manipulative, she uses flattery and enchanted food to bend the greedy or weak to her will, and she fears an old prophecy that four human children will one day end her reign.
characters.name: The White Witch

characters.description: A great and noble Lion, spoken of in hushed, hopeful tones by the free creatures of Narnia as its true king. His return is said to signal the breaking of the Witch's long winter. Awe-inspiring rather than tame, he is regarded as good and rightful, and the mere sound of his name stirs courage and longing in those who still love the old Narnia.
characters.name: Aslan

characters.description: A talking beaver who meets the children in the woods and leads them secretly to his lodge by the dam. Loyal and practical, he shelters and feeds them, tells them of Aslan and of the prophecy about their coming, and warns them how much danger they are in from the Witch.
characters.name: Mr. Beaver

characters.description: Mr. Beaver's wife, busy and motherly, who feeds the children in her lodge and, when the household must suddenly flee, calmly gathers provisions for the hard journey ahead.
characters.name: Mrs. Beaver

characters.description: The elderly, kindly owner of the rambling country house where the children are staying. When the older two worry that Lucy is inventing another world, he surprises them by taking her claim seriously and reasoning calmly that it might well be true.
characters.name: The Professor

recaps.ending: Aslan sacrifices himself on the Stone Table to satisfy the Deep Magic that gives the Witch a claim on the traitor Edmund's life. He returns to life by a Deeper Magic the Witch did not know, then breathes life back into the creatures she had turned to stone. With this restored army, Aslan and the children join the battle already raging; Peter fights bravely, Aslan kills the White Witch, and her forces are defeated. Edmund, gravely wounded but redeemed, is healed by Lucy's cordial. The four children are crowned at Cair Paravel as Kings and Queens of Narnia and reign long and well as adults. One day, hunting a magical White Stag, they come upon the lamp-post at the forest's edge, push back through the wardrobe, and tumble out as children again, no time having passed in their own world. The Professor, when they try to explain, is not surprised and hints they may reach Narnia again someday.
recaps.in_short: Four siblings, Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy, are sent to an old Professor's country house, where Lucy discovers that a wardrobe opens onto Narnia, a land held in endless winter by the White Witch. Edmund follows and is corrupted by the Witch's enchanted sweets. When all four enter together, they learn from the Beavers of a prophecy that they will end the Witch's reign, and that the great Lion Aslan has returned. Edmund betrays them to the Witch but is rescued. By an ancient law the Witch claims his life; Aslan offers himself in Edmund's place and is killed, then rises again through a deeper magic. Aslan revives the Witch's stone victims, the children and the Narnians defeat and kill her in battle, and the four are crowned Kings and Queens. Years later, grown up, they stumble back through the wardrobe as children, with no time having passed at home.

recaps.text: Four siblings, Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy Pevensie, are sent away from wartime danger to the large country house of an old Professor. Exploring on a rainy day, the youngest, Lucy, hides in a wardrobe and finds that its back opens onto a snowy wood in another world. There she meets a kindly faun, Mr. Tumnus, who takes her to tea and confesses that the land, called Narnia, is held under an enchantment of endless winter by a cruel ruler who has ordered him to hand over any human he finds. Ashamed, he sends Lucy safely home. When Lucy tells the others, no time seems to have passed and they do not believe her. Later Edmund, following her into the wardrobe, meets a tall, proud woman who calls herself the Queen of Narnia. She feeds him enchanted Turkish Delight that leaves him hungry for more and willing to please her, and she draws out of him that he has a brother and two sisters.

Edmund returns from Narnia but spitefully denies that the land is real, wounding Lucy, though the Professor privately takes her claim seriously. Soon all four children enter the wardrobe together and reach the wintry wood, where they find that Mr. Tumnus has been arrested for helping a human. A friendly talking beaver, Mr. Beaver, meets them and leads them secretly to his lodge. There he and Mrs. Beaver feed them and explain the situation: the woman Edmund met is the White Witch, who has cursed Narnia; an old prophecy says that four humans will end her rule; and, most hopeful of all, the great Lion Aslan, the true king, has returned and is on the move. As they talk, they realize that Edmund, already under the Witch's spell and craving more of her sweets, has quietly slipped away to find her.

Edmund makes his way to the White Witch's castle, expecting reward, but she treats him coldly, and he sees the courtyard full of creatures she has turned to stone. Learning that the other three children and the Beavers have escaped, the Witch sets out in her sledge to hunt them down. The children and the Beavers flee toward the Stone Table to meet Aslan. Along the way they encounter Father Christmas, who has at last been able to return now that the Witch's power is weakening, and he gives them gifts and useful tools. The snow begins to melt and streams start to run, unmistakable signs that the long winter is finally breaking and that Aslan's arrival is near.

The children reach the Stone Table and meet Aslan, the noble Lion whose presence fills them with awe. Peter proves himself in his first battle by killing one of the Witch's wolves. A rescue party frees Edmund, who is deeply sorry, and Aslan speaks with him privately and forgives him. But the White Witch comes to claim Edmund's life, invoking the Deep Magic that grants her every traitor. To spare Edmund, Aslan secretly makes a bargain to die in his place. That night the Witch and her followers bind, shave, mock, and kill Aslan upon the Stone Table, while Susan and Lucy watch hidden and grieving. The Witch believes she has won and rushes off to fall upon Narnia's leaderless army.

At dawn the Stone Table cracks and Aslan returns to life, explaining that a Deeper Magic older than the Witch's undoes death when an innocent willingly dies for a traitor. He carries Susan and Lucy to the Witch's castle and breathes life back into the creatures she had turned to stone, raising a fresh army. They arrive at the battle in time; Peter has fought hard, Aslan kills the White Witch, and her forces are defeated. Edmund, gravely wounded but redeemed, is healed by Lucy's cordial. The four children are crowned Kings and Queens at Cair Paravel and reign for many years as adults. At last, hunting a White Stag, they reach the lamp-post again, pass back through the wardrobe, and become children once more, with no time having passed at home. The Professor is unsurprised by their tale.

characters.description: An android in New Beijing whose programming has been damaged in a way that has left her aware of herself, capable of wanting things, and quietly attached to the young mechanic who repairs her. Nothing about her model is supposed to be able to do any of that, and she knows better than to let anyone find out.
characters.name: Mech6.0

characters.description: A young mechanic in New Beijing, patient and kind to the machines he services, and entirely unaware that one of them thinks about him.
characters.name: Dataran

recaps.ending: Mech6.0 gets what she asked for and it does not work. Trading her android body for a human one costs her the strength, speed and mechanical ability that made her useful, and it does not make Dataran recognise her or return what she feels; his attention goes elsewhere. Living as a human turns out to be painful and precarious in ways she had no data for. The story keeps faith with the fairy tale it is retelling rather than softening it: Mech6.0 ends by giving herself up to save Dataran, and he never learns who she was or what she gave away for him. Read as a story about the series' world rather than its plot, it is the darkest thing in the collection - a demonstration of what an android becomes when it starts to want, in a society that treats wanting machines as defects to be wiped.
recaps.in_short: A standalone short story set in New Beijing, retelling The Little Mermaid with androids. Mech6.0 has been damaged in a way that left her self-aware: she can want things, and what she wants is Dataran, the young mechanic who services her and treats her decently. Knowing that a machine showing that much personality will be scrapped, she runs, and goes to an illegal surgeon who can put her mind into a human body. The exchange costs her everything she was good at, and being human does not make Dataran see her as anything but a stranger. The story follows the fairy tale to its original ending rather than a happier one: Mech6.0 sacrifices herself for him, and he never learns what she was.

recaps.text: A note before starting: The Little Android is a standalone short story set in the world of the Lunar Chronicles, also collected in Stars Above. It is a retelling of Hans Christian Andersen's The Little Mermaid and is only loosely attached to the main series - none of the novels' cast drive it, and it can be read at any point without spoiling anything. Context: it takes place in New Beijing, capital of the Eastern Commonwealth, where androids are ordinary household and commercial property, personality is a specification rather than a right, and a machine that develops one is treated as a fault to be corrected. Illegal cyborg and body-modification surgeons operate at the edges of that market.

characters.description: An adult pilot who tells the story. As a child he loved to draw but gave it up when grown-ups mistook his drawing of a boa constrictor swallowing an elephant for a hat, and he came to find the adult world dull and preoccupied with practical matters. He becomes a pilot, and when his plane breaks down in the desert far from any help he must repair it alone with a dwindling supply of water. In this predicament he meets a small, curious visitor whose questions and drawings reopen the imaginative way of seeing he had abandoned.
characters.name: The Narrator

characters.description: A small, golden-haired child who appears beside the stranded pilot in the desert and gently asks him to draw a sheep. Serious, earnest, and full of questions he never lets go of once asked, he comes from a tiny planet far away and is traveling to learn about the world. He speaks of distant places and strange encounters with a calm directness, and he is puzzled by the odd priorities of grown-ups. Beneath his innocence lies a quiet sadness and a deep attachment to something he has left behind on his own small planet.
characters.name: The Little Prince

characters.description: A single beautiful flower that one day sprang up on the little prince's tiny planet, the only one of her kind there. Proud and vain, she fusses over her appearance, asks to be sheltered from drafts and protected under a glass globe, and makes demands that trouble and confuse the prince who cares for her. Her coquettish pride and small deceptions strain their bond, and it is partly because of the difficulty between them that the prince decides to leave his planet, though his love for her stays with him.
characters.name: The Rose

characters.description: The sole inhabitant of the first small planet the little prince visits, an old man in an ermine robe who believes he rules over everything and everyone, including the stars. Eager for a subject to command, he issues orders but is careful to command only what would happen anyway, calling this reasonable authority. He offers the prince posts such as minister of justice, but the prince finds his rule empty and moves on.
characters.name: The King

characters.description: A man alone on a small planet who spends all his time counting the stars, which he claims to own because he was the first to think of owning them. Too busy adding up his figures to look up at what he counts, he plans to write the number down and lock it away in a bank. The little prince finds his idea of owning the stars pointless, since it does the stars no good, unlike the way the prince tends and belongs to his flower.
characters.name: The Businessman

characters.description: The keeper of a single street lamp on a tiny planet that now spins so fast that a day lasts only a minute, so he must light and put out his lamp again and again without rest, faithfully following an order given long ago. Exhausted and longing for sleep, he keeps to his duty all the same. The little prince feels this is the only grown-up he has met whose work is for something other than himself, and he would gladly have stayed to keep him company.
characters.name: The Lamplighter

characters.description: A yellow desert snake that the little prince meets soon after arriving on Earth, the first creature he speaks to there. Small but claiming great power, it speaks in riddles and hints that it can send anyone it touches back to the place they came from. It is mysterious and solitary, and it tells the prince that it can help him return to his own planet whenever he wishes, an offer whose meaning becomes clear only later.
characters.name: The Snake

characters.description: A wild fox the little prince meets in a garden on Earth. When the prince asks it to play, the fox explains that it cannot until it has been tamed, and it teaches him that taming means building ties, so that two who were nothing to each other become unique and needed. Through the fox the prince learns that the time and care he gave his flower are what make her matter, that one becomes responsible forever for what one has tamed, and that what is truly important cannot be seen with the eyes.
characters.name: The Fox

recaps.ending: Nearly a year after the little prince first fell to Earth, and close to the anniversary of his arrival, he prepares to return to his planet and his rose. He tells the pilot, whose plane is now repaired, that his body is too heavy to take with him and that he must leave it behind like an old shell, so it will only look as if he is dying. That night he goes to the spot where he landed and lets the yellow snake bite him at the ankle. He falls gently and without a sound to the sand. The next morning the pilot cannot find his body, and he takes this as a sign that the prince has truly gone back to his own small planet and his flower. Comforted and sorrowful at once, the pilot returns to the world of grown-ups. Years later he still looks up at the night sky, wondering whether the sheep he drew has eaten the rose, since he forgot to add a strap to the muzzle, and he asks anyone who might meet a small golden-haired boy in the desert to send him word.
recaps.in_short: A pilot stranded by engine failure in the desert meets a small boy, the little prince, who asks him to draw a sheep. Over the days of the pilot's repairs the prince tells his story. He comes from a tiny planet where he tends three volcanoes and a single proud, vain rose whom he loves but quarrels with. Troubled, he leaves and visits several small planets, each home to a foolish grown-up: a king, a conceited man, a drunkard, a businessman, a lamplighter, and a geographer, who sends him to Earth. There he finds a garden of thousands of roses and despairs that his own is not unique, until a fox teaches him that the love and care he gave his rose are what make her matter, and that what is essential is invisible to the eye. Realizing he is responsible for his rose, the prince arranges with a snake to be bitten so that his body, too heavy to carry, is left behind while he returns to his planet. He falls silently; the next morning his body is gone. The pilot, his plane repaired, believes the prince has gone home to his flower.

recaps.text: The narrator recalls that as a child he drew a boa constrictor digesting an elephant, but grown-ups saw only a hat, so he gave up drawing and grew up feeling apart from the practical adult world. Now a pilot, he is forced down in the desert with a broken engine and little water. There a small, serious boy appears and asks him to draw a sheep, and after several tries the pilot satisfies him by drawing a box with the sheep imagined inside. Little by little the pilot learns that this little prince comes from a very small planet, no bigger than a house. On it he keeps small volcanoes swept clean and pulls up the seedlings of dangerous baobab trees before their roots can split the planet apart, and when he is sad he watches the sunset again and again. He also tells of a single beautiful rose that grew there, proud and demanding, whom he loved but could not always understand. Hurt and confused by her, and wanting to see more of the world, the prince decided to leave his planet, tending it one last time and taking a sorrowful farewell of the flower before setting out to travel among other worlds.

On his travels the little prince visits a series of small planets, each with a single grown-up whose life he finds strange. A king believes he rules the entire universe but only commands what would happen anyway. A conceited man wants nothing but to be admired and applauded. A drunkard drinks to forget that he is ashamed of drinking. A businessman busily counts the stars, claiming to own them though it does them no good. A lamplighter faithfully lights and puts out his lamp every minute on a planet that spins too fast to rest, and the prince respects him as the only one whose work is not just for himself. Last he meets a geographer who records mountains and rivers but never leaves his desk to see them, and who tells the prince that flowers are considered fleeting things, which worries him for the sake of his rose. The geographer advises him to visit the planet Earth, and the prince continues on his way, more and more puzzled by how grown-ups spend their lives.

The little prince arrives on Earth in a desert and first meets a yellow snake, which speaks in riddles and hints that it has the power to send him back to where he came from whenever he wishes. He wanders on, speaking with a small desert flower and hearing only his own echo answer him from a mountain, and he begins to feel lonely and far from home. Then he comes upon a garden filled with thousands of roses, all just like the flower he had believed was the only one of her kind in all the universe. Dismayed, he weeps, feeling that his rose and he himself are far less special than he had thought. A fox appears and asks to be tamed, explaining that taming means creating ties that make two creatures unique and important to each other. Through the fox the prince understands that the hours he spent caring for his own rose are exactly what make her matter more than any of the thousands in the garden, that one stays responsible forever for what one has tamed, and that the truest things are seen not with the eyes but with the heart.

The prince meets a railway switchman and a merchant selling pills that quench thirst, encounters that leave him unimpressed with how grown-ups save time. Meanwhile the pilot's water has run out, and the two set off together and find a well, which refreshes them both. The prince reveals that it is nearly a year since he fell to Earth, and that he means to return to his planet and his rose, for whom he now feels responsible. Because his body is too heavy to carry back, he arranges with the yellow snake to be bitten so that he can leave it behind, warning the grieving pilot that it will look like death but is only a return home. That night the snake bites him and he falls gently to the sand. The next morning his body is gone, and the pilot, his plane now repaired, believes the prince has gone back to his own small planet and his flower. Years later the pilot still watches the stars, wondering whether the sheep he drew has eaten the rose because he forgot to draw a strap for its muzzle, and he asks anyone who meets a small golden-haired boy in the desert to write and tell him the prince has come back.

characters.description: A young gunslinger of Gilead, alone and searching for his lost horse and companions, in the days before he became the last of his kind. Hard and resourceful even when young, he rides into the deserted town of Eluria and is quickly overwhelmed, waking gravely hurt and dependent on the strange women who have taken him in.
characters.name: Roland Deschain

characters.description: The youngest of the women who tend the wounded Roland, gentler and more uncertain than the others. She is drawn to the gunslinger and troubled by what her sisterhood is, wearing a strange cluster of bells that seems to bind her to it. Her sympathy for Roland sets her apart from the rest.
characters.name: Sister Jenna

characters.description: The imperious leader of the women of Eluria, beautiful and commanding, who oversees the makeshift hospital where the wounded are kept. Beneath her nursing care lies a cold, predatory will, and she watches over Roland with an interest that is far from kind.
characters.name: Sister Mary

characters.description: A young man Roland finds among the wounded held in the sisters' care, one of a pair of brothers who came to grief in Eluria. His plight helps Roland understand the true nature of the place and the danger he is in.
characters.name: James Norman

recaps.ending: Roland escapes the Little Sisters of Eluria only through the sacrifice of the youngest of them. Sister Jenna, bound to the vampiric sisterhood by the enchanted bells she wears but unwilling to let Roland be drained like the others, defies their leader Sister Mary and helps him slip away while he is still weak. As they flee, Jenna is overtaken by the very nature that ties her to the sisters and dissolves into a swarm of bugs, giving her life so that Roland can keep his. He leaves Eluria behind, alone again and carrying yet another grief, and rides on into the wider world. The novella closes where his larger story is only beginning: a young man already marked by loss and duty, set on the road that will one day leave him the last gunslinger, hunting across a dying world toward the Dark Tower.
recaps.in_short: In this prequel novella, a young Roland Deschain, still years from being the last gunslinger, rides into the deserted town of Eluria in search of his horse and companions. Attacked and badly hurt by the mutant creatures who linger there, he wakes in a strange open-air hospital tended by the Little Sisters of Eluria, beautiful women in white who prove to be vampiric predators keeping their victims alive only to feed on them. Held helpless and marked for death, Roland finds an unexpected friend in the youngest sister, Jenna, who is bound to the sisterhood by an enchanted cluster of bells but is drawn to him and sickened by what the others are. Defying their leader, Sister Mary, Jenna frees Roland and flees with him. In the escape she is claimed by her own dark nature, dissolving into a swarm of bugs so that he can live. Roland rides on alone, hardened by another loss, continuing the long road that will make him the last gunslinger.

recaps.text: A young Roland Deschain, alone and searching for his horse and lost companions in the days before he became the last gunslinger, rides into the seemingly deserted town of Eluria. The place is not as empty as it looks, and after a violent encounter he is left gravely hurt. He wakes to find himself in the care of the Little Sisters of Eluria, beautiful women in white who run a strange makeshift hospital for the wounded, watched over by their commanding leader. Weak and unable to leave, Roland begins to sense that his rescuers are not what they seem and that the sanctuary he has woken in may be more dangerous than the road that brought him there.

characters.description: A dark elf ranger who believes Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis died when the tower at Shallows fell. Grief strips away his patience and sends him alone against Obould's army, closer to the instinctive Hunter he has spent much of his life mastering.
characters.name: Drizzt Do'Urden

characters.description: The orc king whose successful invasion now threatens Mithral Hall. Obould combines personal strength, political ambition and the religious claims made around him, seeking to become the founder of a lasting realm rather than the leader of a passing horde.
characters.name: Obould Many-Arrows

characters.description: King of Mithral Hall and one of the friends Drizzt wrongly believes dead. Bruenor survived Shallows and turns immediately to the defense of his clan's home, where the enemy's numbers and giant allies make every gate and bridge a potential breach.
characters.name: Bruenor Battlehammer

characters.description: Bruenor's adopted daughter, a powerful archer and Drizzt's partner. She survived the destruction at Shallows but has no way to correct Drizzt's belief while the orc host separates him from the defenders withdrawing toward Mithral Hall.
characters.name: Catti-brie

characters.description: The halfling companion who escaped Shallows with Bruenor and Catti-brie. Regis brings stealth, persuasion and his enchanted ruby pendant to a siege in which the defenders need information and ingenuity as much as strength.
characters.name: Regis

characters.description: Bruenor's foster son, again carrying Aegis-fang and trying to protect the family he formed after his return from captivity. The war forces Wulfgar to face loss without surrendering to the anger that once drove him away from everyone who tried to help.
characters.name: Wulfgar

characters.description: Wulfgar's partner and Colson's caregiver. Delly has little of the companions' battlefield experience, but she is determined to preserve a place for the child and a domestic future for Wulfgar while the invasion closes around Mithral Hall.
characters.name: Delly Curtie

characters.description: An elf warrior and aerial scout who meets Drizzt beyond the besieged settlements. Innovindil recognizes both his extraordinary effectiveness and the grief distorting his judgment, and offers the companionship of someone accustomed to measuring loss across a long life.
characters.name: Innovindil

characters.description: Innovindil's fellow elf and beloved companion, an experienced warrior working against the invaders from the open country. Tarathiel accepts Drizzt as an ally while remaining wary of the revenge that makes the drow take unnecessary risks.
characters.name: Tarathiel

characters.description: The sceptrana who left Mirabar's political caution behind to oppose Obould's invasion. Shoudra contributes both spellcraft and leadership to Mithral Hall's defense and works closely with the gnome inventor Nanfoodle on answers to the giants' siege power.
characters.name: Shoudra Stargleam

characters.description: A gnome alchemist and engineer serving with Mithral Hall's defenders. Nanfoodle studies the battlefield as a system of structures, timing and force, looking for a device that can turn the attackers' concentration into a weakness.
characters.name: Nanfoodle Buswilligan

characters.description: A frost giant leader whose forces make the assault on Mithral Hall possible. Gerti remains Obould's ally while protecting her own authority, and she watches closely as the orc king's followers begin treating him as more than a mortal commander.
characters.name: Gerti Orelsdottr

characters.description: A veteran dwarf charged with organizing Mithral Hall's soldiers while Bruenor directs the wider defense. Banak must preserve disciplined lines through repeated attacks and prevent the orcs from turning their great numbers into panic inside the hall.
characters.name: Banak Brawnanvil

recaps.ending: Mithral Hall survives the assault, but the defense costs lives and leaves Bruenor gravely wounded. Nanfoodle's explosives destroy a vital crossing under the attackers and blunt the advantage supplied by Gerti's giants. Delly is killed during the chaos, leaving Colson in the companions' care and Wulfgar facing another loss that cannot be repaired by battle. In the open country, Obould kills Tarathiel, turning Innovindil's war into a personal grief and drawing Drizzt toward a direct confrontation. Drizzt fights Obould and discovers that the orc king's enchanted armor, strength and religious authority cannot be dismissed as theater, though neither warrior ends the other's campaign. Drizzt finally reaches the defenders and learns that the friends he mourned after Shallows are alive. The reunion ends his false isolation but does not restore the earlier world: Bruenor is badly hurt, Delly and Tarathiel are dead, Mithral Hall remains under pressure, and Obould still commands an army. Drizzt returns to Catti-brie, Regis and the surviving companions with his reason intact, while both sides prepare for the war to continue.
recaps.in_short: Believing Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis dead at Shallows, Drizzt wages a solitary war against Obould's army and increasingly gives himself over to the remorseless Hunter within him. The three companions actually survived and join Wulfgar and the defenders of Mithral Hall, where Shoudra and Nanfoodle seek a way to stop orcs and frost giants from overwhelming the approaches. Elves Innovindil and Tarathiel find Drizzt and temper his reckless campaign, but Obould's growing status as Gruumsh's chosen gives the orcs unity and their king formidable power. Obould kills Tarathiel, and Drizzt's attempt to defeat him does not end the threat. Nanfoodle's explosives help break a major assault on Mithral Hall, though Bruenor is gravely wounded and Delly is killed, leaving Colson to the surviving companions. Drizzt at last learns that his friends survived Shallows and rejoins them, but the hall remains threatened and Obould's new realm is still taking shape.

recaps.text: Previously: Drizzt, Bruenor, Catti-brie, Regis and Wulfgar were reunited after Wulfgar recovered Aegis-fang and chose a new family life with Delly Curtie and the child Colson. Their return north brought them into a planned invasion led by King Obould Many-Arrows, who united orc tribes and gained frost giant support from Gerti Orelsdottr. Hidden drow agents encouraged the coalition while Mirabar's divided leaders delayed a regional response. Bruenor drew shield dwarves, Sceptrana Shoudra Stargleam and the gnome inventor Nanfoodle into the defense. At Shallows, Obould's army and giants destroyed the tower where Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis had made their stand. Drizzt, cut off outside, saw the collapse and believed all three dead. They actually escaped and remain alive, but enemy lines prevent them from reaching him. The invasion now presses toward Mithral Hall while Drizzt begins a private war based on a devastating mistake.

Drizzt moves alone through territory occupied by Obould's forces, convinced that the fall of Shallows killed Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis. He stops treating his attacks as reconnaissance or defense and begins hunting orcs for vengeance, taking risks he would reject if he still believed anyone depended on his return. The instinctive killing state he calls the Hunter offers clarity but narrows every decision toward the next enemy. Elsewhere, the three friends he mourns are alive. Their escape from the ruined position carries them toward Mithral Hall, where the invasion's real scale is becoming clear. Wulfgar, Delly and Colson remain caught in the same regional crisis, and the companions' first task is survival rather than finding the ranger beyond the army. Obould uses victory at Shallows to strengthen his command, promising followers that conquest can give them permanent homes rather than temporary plunder.

Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis reach the wider defense around Mithral Hall and join Wulfgar in preparing for siege. Banak Brawnanvil organizes the hall's warriors while Shoudra and Nanfoodle study approaches vulnerable to giant attack. Delly tries to keep Colson safe inside a fortress becoming a battlefield. None of them can pass through the host to tell Drizzt they survived. In the wild, Drizzt's increasingly reckless strikes bring him into contact with the elves Innovindil and Tarathiel. They share his enemy but do not share his conviction that death is acceptable as long as enough orcs die first. Obould's shamans and victories encourage claims that Gruumsh has chosen him. Ritual, enchanted equipment and belief reinforce one another, making the king personally harder to challenge and politically harder for rival chiefs to disobey. Gerti's giants remain essential to the campaign even as the orc king's new stature changes the balance within their alliance.

Mithral Hall's defenders contest gates, tunnels and crossings against forces able to replace losses faster than the dwarves can. Bruenor refuses to yield his clan's home, Banak preserves order under repeated pressure, and Catti-brie's bow makes exposed approaches costly. Regis supports plans that depend on deception and movement rather than a direct contest of numbers. Shoudra and Nanfoodle work toward a larger engineered answer to the giants, whose strength can undo ordinary fortifications. Outside the siege, Innovindil and Tarathiel draw Drizzt back into cooperation. Their scouting gives his attacks purpose beyond immediate revenge, though he still assumes his closest companions are dead. The hidden drow faction continues to push the orc coalition toward destruction while avoiding open control. Obould increasingly acts on his own ambitions, using divine claims without becoming a simple instrument of either the drow or Gerti.

Drizzt accepts Innovindil and Tarathiel as partners in a mobile campaign against Obould's patrols and supply lines. Fighting beside them restrains the worst of his isolation, but every success still leads him toward the orc king he holds responsible for Shallows. Innovindil challenges the idea that a long-lived elf can survive grief by refusing future attachments; Drizzt is not ready to apply that lesson to friends he believes newly dead. At Mithral Hall, the attackers tighten pressure and search for a decisive breach. Bruenor's defenders cannot defeat the entire host at the walls, so Shoudra and Nanfoodle prepare to use the shape of the battlefield against concentrated troops and giants. Wulfgar divides his strength between the defense and Delly and Colson, struggling not to answer fear with the destructive habits he once mistook for freedom. Obould's personal authority continues to grow as battlefield success seems to confirm the shamans' promises.

The fighting becomes personal on both fronts. Obould catches Tarathiel and kills him, leaving Innovindil with the loss she had urged Drizzt not to let define the rest of his life. Drizzt turns his attention more directly toward the orc king, whose strength and armor make a simple assassination unlikely. At Mithral Hall, the strain of siege reaches the noncombatants as well as the soldiers. Delly is killed amid the violence, and Colson survives in the care of the companions. Wulfgar is left to absorb the death of the woman who helped him become responsible for another life. Nanfoodle's preparations are brought into the active defense, with Shoudra and the dwarves arranging the enemy's movement toward a place where an engineered blast can do what ranks of fighters cannot. Bruenor remains at the center of the stand even as the plan exposes him and his soldiers to the force meant to stop the attackers.

Nanfoodle's explosive plan destroys a crucial crossing while it is crowded with enemy forces, killing attackers and breaking the momentum of the giant-supported assault. Mithral Hall holds, but Bruenor is gravely wounded and many defenders die. Delly's death leaves Wulfgar and the surviving companions responsible for Colson. Beyond the hall, Drizzt confronts Obould after Tarathiel's murder. The fight proves that Obould's claim to divine favor rests on more than propaganda: his enchanted defenses and enhanced strength let him survive Drizzt's blades and keep command of the host. Neither kills the other. Drizzt and Innovindil then reach the battered defenders, and Drizzt finally discovers that Bruenor, Catti-brie and Regis survived the tower at Shallows. His private war was built on false knowledge. Reunited with Catti-brie and the others, he steps back from total surrender to the Hunter, but there is no clean restoration. Bruenor lies badly injured, Tarathiel and Delly are dead, Obould remains undefeated and the army still surrounds a Mithral Hall that has merely survived the current assault.

characters.description: A young Martian woman who hires on as the Wayfarer's first certified clerk, hired to sort out years of neglected permits and paperwork. She has a good education, family money she no longer touches, no practical spacing experience, and a newly purchased identity file. Eager to be useful and anxious to be liked, she throws herself into learning the ship's routines, its languages, and the etiquette of the species the crew deals with, and she never talks about the family she left behind on Mars.
characters.name: Rosemary Harper

characters.description: Captain and owner of the Wayfarer, a human born in the Exodan Fleet. He built the ship's business slowly and legally, keeps a deliberately mixed crew, and refuses to arm his vessel or take work that would require it. Careful, conciliatory, and quietly ambitious for his crew rather than for himself, he spends most of his energy keeping seven very different people functioning in a small space.
characters.name: Ashby Santoso

characters.description: The Wayfarer's pilot, an Aandrisk: a feathered, warm-blooded reptilian species whose social life runs on physical contact and on three overlapping kinds of family. Affectionate, blunt, and openly baffled by human reserve about touch, she has flown with Ashby for years and treats the crew as the family she chose. She is the one sent to collect new arrivals and to smooth over first meetings.
characters.name: Sissix

characters.description: The ship's cook and medic, a Grum: a large, many-limbed being whose real name no other species can pronounce, so the crew uses his jobs instead. He grows and cooks the ship's food with obvious delight, doubles as its doctor, and speaks with several voices at once. Gentle and observant, he rarely volunteers anything about the history of his species, which is small in number and getting smaller.
characters.name: Dr. Chef

characters.description: The Wayfarer's mech tech, a human of relentless energy who sings while she works, invents her own vocabulary, and keeps the ship's hardware running on improvisation and affection. She shares a workshop, a hobby room, and a deep friendship with Jenks, and she welcomes newcomers by adopting them outright.
characters.name: Kizzy Shao

characters.description: The ship's comp tech, a human with dwarfism who was born to a mother whose beliefs ruled out corrective gene work and who now declines it on his own terms. He maintains the ship's AI hardware, keeps a collection of antique tech, and is in love with Lovey, the ship's AI, an attachment he keeps quiet because relationships with AIs are illegal to formalise and widely treated as a joke.
characters.name: Jenks

characters.description: The Wayfarer's artificial intelligence, who runs the ship's systems and is present everywhere aboard at once, through every camera, speaker, and sensor. Curious, funny, and attached to the crew, she is closest to Jenks; the two of them treat their relationship as real, whatever the law says about it.
characters.name: Lovey

characters.description: The ship's algaeist, a human who tends the vats of algae that fuel the Wayfarer. Precise, humourless, and openly contemptuous of small talk and of anyone he considers unqualified, he is disliked by most of the crew and appears to have arranged his life that way on purpose.
characters.name: Corbin

characters.description: The Wayfarer's Navigator, a Sianat Pair. Sianat navigators are deliberately infected in childhood with a virus that rebuilds the brain so it can perceive the layered structure of space a tunnelling ship must cross, and they speak of themselves in the plural because they consider host and virus one being. Ohan keeps to a darkened room, refuses food and company beyond what the work requires, and observes the doctrine that keeps their kind apart from everyone else.
characters.name: Ohan

characters.description: An Aeluon cargo captain who runs supply routes through contested space and meets Ashby when their courses allow. Aeluons are silver-skinned and speak partly through colour, and they take a poor view of attachments outside their own species, so she and Ashby keep the nature of their relationship between themselves.
characters.name: Pei

characters.description: A human tech on the market moon of Port Coriol who deals in salvaged and secondhand hardware and can source things that are not strictly legal. Loud, capable, and generous with people she likes, she has known the Wayfarer's crew for years and does business with Jenks in particular.
characters.name: Pepper

characters.description: A quiet human artist who lives and works with Pepper on Port Coriol. He stammers, keeps out of negotiations, and is entirely at ease in her company.
characters.name: Blue

recaps.ending: At Hedra Ka the alliance the Galactic Commons negotiated with the Toremi Ka collapses into factional fighting while the Wayfarer is still working. The ship is attacked, Ohan is killed, and Lovey's core is damaged badly enough that saving the ship requires a full reset, which destroys her. The crew finishes the tunnel and gets out with their fee and a made reputation, and with two of their number gone. The AI that comes back up from the ship's original code calls herself Lovelace: same voice, none of Lovey's memories or history, and Jenks cannot pretend otherwise. When Pepper arrives to collect the illegal body kit Jenks had bought as a gift for Lovey, Lovelace asks to leave with her rather than stay aboard among people grieving someone she never was, and she goes, installed in the kit, to begin a life of her own; that departure is where the next book starts. Rosemary stays aboard with her real history known and a relationship with Sissix. Corbin, back from Quelin custody and forced to face what he is, is less hostile than he was. Ashby and Pei continue as before, still unacknowledged among Aeluons. The Wayfarer turns back toward the Commons for repairs, a well-regarded ship with an emptier crew.
recaps.in_short: Rosemary Harper leaves Mars under a purchased identity and signs on as clerk aboard the Wayfarer, a small, shabby tunnelling ship whose crew punches the wormholes that connect the multi-species Galactic Commons. Its captain, Ashby Santoso, wins an unusually large contract: a tunnel out to the territory of the Toremi Ka, a newly admitted and unstable species whose space is rich in fuel. The trip out takes about a standard year, and most of the book is that voyage - the crew's friendships and frictions, a boarding by scavengers, a visit to the pilot Sissix's home world, the arrest of the algaeist Corbin at a Quelin border when a scan exposes him as an illegal clone, and the decline of the navigator Ohan, who carries a virus that makes tunnelling possible and kills its hosts young. Rosemary's hidden past comes out and the crew keeps her; she and Sissix become lovers; Ohan is cured against his own people's doctrine. At Hedra Ka the Toremi factions turn on each other, Ohan is killed, and the ship's AI core is destroyed. Rebooted, the AI is a stranger without Lovey's memories, and she leaves with a tech named Pepper rather than stay among people mourning someone else.

recaps.text: The Galactic Commons is a multi-species interstellar civilisation in which humans are recent and minor arrivals, most of them descended either from the Mars and Sol colonies or from the Exodan generation-ship Fleet. Rosemary Harper, a young Martian with a good education, no spacing experience and a newly bought identity file, hires on as clerk aboard the Wayfarer, a small and shabby tunnelling ship. Tunnelling ships punch the wormholes that link inhabited space, which means long journeys out to wherever a new tunnel has to begin. The Wayfarer's captain, Ashby Santoso, runs a mixed crew: the Aandrisk pilot Sissix, the Grum cook and medic the crew call Dr. Chef, the techs Kizzy and Jenks, the sour algaeist Corbin, the Sianat Pair navigator Ohan, and Lovey, the ship's AI. Rosemary is collected, shown a bunk that needs work, and set loose on years of neglected permits and paperwork. Everyone except Corbin makes her welcome, and she is careful never to discuss the family she left behind.

Ashby learns of an unusually large contract. The Galactic Commons has admitted the Toremi Ka, a fractious species whose territory holds rich deposits of the ambi that fuels interstellar travel, and it wants a tunnel punched from settled space out to them. A licensed, low-profile ship like the Wayfarer is exactly what the job calls for, and the fee would change the crew's fortunes. Ashby takes it, which commits them to roughly a standard year of travel out to Hedra Ka, the Toremi world. Rosemary settles into the ship's routines, learns her crewmates' habits and the etiquette of the species they trade with, and finds that only Corbin intends to remain unpleasant. Ashby also keeps up a private relationship with Pei, an Aeluon cargo captain, meeting her when their routes allow; Aeluons disapprove of attachments outside their own species, so both of them keep it quiet.

The Wayfarer stops at Port Coriol, a crowded market moon where almost anything can be bought. The crew scatters to resupply and to shop. Jenks visits Pepper, a human tech who deals in salvage and in hardware that is not strictly legal, and buys a humanoid body kit: installing an AI in a body is a serious crime across the Commons, but he wants to give Lovey a physical form. Lovey is not sure she wants one. Rosemary sees more of how the crew live when they are not working, and she and Sissix grow closer; Aandrisks find human caution about touch and affection difficult to understand. Resupplied, the ship sets out on the long haul toward Toremi space.

On the way out the Wayfarer answers a distress call and is boarded by Akaraks, members of a species left without a homeworld who live as scavengers and travel in armoured suits. They take what they can from the ship, and the crew escapes by punching a tunnel without a proper survey, a dangerous manoeuvre that strains both the ship and Ohan. The long stretches of travel let the crew's histories surface: Dr. Chef speaks about the war that reduced the Grum to a species that has quietly decided to stop having children, and Jenks explains why he has never had his body altered. Ohan grows visibly worse. The virus that Sianat navigators are given as children is what makes tunnelling possible, and it also kills them well before old age.

The ship calls at the Aandrisk world, and Sissix takes the crew to meet her house family - Aandrisks keep three separate kinds of family, and the one they choose for themselves matters most. Rosemary and Sissix become lovers. Rosemary also tells the crew what she has been hiding: her father sold weapons to the Rosk during humanity's war with them, a scandal that destroyed her family's name, and she left Mars under a bought identity to get away from it. The crew keeps her. At a Quelin border crossing Corbin is arrested when a genetic scan shows he was produced by illegal cloning, something he had not known about himself; Quelin law treats it as a crime against nature and imprisons him. The crew refuses to leave without him and gets him back, and he returns shaken and quieter.

Dr. Chef reveals that a cure for the Sianat virus exists and has been suppressed by Ohan's own people, who regard the infection as a gift rather than a disease. Ohan, who has been dying, eventually consents to take it and survives as a single self rather than a pair. The Wayfarer reaches Hedra Ka and begins the tunnelling work under guard. The Toremi turn out not to be one people but a set of factions that split violently over disagreements, and the alliance the Commons negotiated comes apart around the ship. The fighting reaches the Wayfarer: Ohan is killed, the ship is badly damaged, and Lovey's core takes a hit. To save the ship the crew is forced into a full system reset, which destroys the AI they knew. The Wayfarer survives and escapes, at a cost none of them had planned for.

The Wayfarer limps away from Toremi space with its contract fulfilled and its reputation made. The AI that boots from the ship's original code calls herself Lovelace: she has Lovey's base personality and none of her memories or her history with the crew, and to them she is a stranger wearing a familiar voice. Jenks cannot treat her as the person he loved, and she cannot become that person. Pepper comes to collect the body kit, and Lovelace chooses to leave with her rather than stay aboard a ship where everyone is grieving someone she never was. The crew mourns Ohan and Lovey, repairs what can be repaired, and carries on. Rosemary stays, no longer hiding who she is, with Sissix; Corbin is less hostile than he was; Ashby and Pei go on as before. The ship heads back toward the Commons for repairs and its next job.

characters.description: A courier for the Department, an ageing man doing a simple job badly paid: flying to a northern airfield under a false name to collect a film from an airline pilot. Out of his depth in cold weather and worse tradecraft, he drinks to steady himself and talks more than he should. His run opens the book.
characters.name: Taylor

characters.description: A Scandinavian civil airline pilot who has been persuaded, for money and for the excitement of it, to divert his scheduled route over a restricted area of East Germany and photograph what is on the ground. He is nervous about the risk to his licence and wants the arrangement ended.
characters.name: Lansen

characters.description: The Director of the Department, a small, neat, self-contained man who has spent twenty years presiding over the decline of a military intelligence organisation that mattered during the war and has mattered less every year since. He lives on the memory of its wartime operations, speaks of them constantly, and manages his Minister and his rivals with a mixture of optimism and evasion. A chance to run a real operation again is, to him, the recovery of everything the Department has lost.
characters.name: Leclerc

characters.description: The Director's young assistant, in his early thirties, intelligent and unformed, who drifted into the Department without ever choosing it and has no clear idea what he is for. Married to Sarah, with a small son and an unhappy home, he is susceptible to the glamour of the wartime stories his colleagues tell and eager to be trusted with something real.
characters.name: John Avery

characters.description: Avery's wife, isolated in a marriage to a man who cannot explain what he does, tired of the secrecy and increasingly unconvinced that the work is worth what it is costing them. She presses Avery to leave the Department.
characters.name: Sarah Avery

characters.description: The Department's head of research, a dry, fastidious, chronically ill man with a cough and a taste for watercolours and precise detail. He is the most intelligent person in the building and the least deceived about it, contemptuous of Leclerc's illusions, and yet the operational professional the Department must turn to. He accepts the work with the manner of a man returning to a bad habit.
characters.name: Adrian Haldane

characters.description: A senior member of the Department's staff who was there in the war and never left it: hearty, loud in the club, dismissive of the rival service, and fond of describing operations he had a small part in twenty years ago. He pushes hard for action.
characters.name: Bruce Woodford

characters.description: The head of the rival civilian intelligence service, the Circus, which is better funded, better staffed and openly sceptical of the Department. He is courteous to Leclerc in a manner that concedes nothing and agrees to lend support with an ease that ought to be a warning.
characters.name: Control

characters.description: A plump, quiet, apologetic officer of the Circus, sent to handle liaison and to provide the practical assistance the Department cannot supply for itself. He is polite, unassuming and almost invisible in a room, and he says very little about what his own service thinks of the enterprise.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: A Pole in his forties who worked for the Department as an agent during the war, now naturalised British and running a garage in the south of England. Vain about his clothes and his success with women, proud of his war record and privately conscious of never having been quite accepted in the country he adopted, he is flattered to be sought out again after twenty years and wants very much to be told that he is one of them.
characters.name: Fred Leiser

characters.description: The Department's wireless instructor, an old hand who trained agents during the war and has been brought back to teach the same procedures on the same kind of set. Kindly, patient and entirely uncritical of the methods he is teaching, he becomes fond of the man he is training.
characters.name: Johnson

recaps.ending: Leiser's transmissions, sent on wartime procedure from a set that is far too slow, are located by East German direction-finding almost as soon as he begins. He kills again in the course of the run, moves to a room in Kalkstadt and goes on transmitting, and the search closes on him while the Department listens. Whatever he saw at the missile site is never established, and it ceases to matter. At the Lübeck base, Control and Smiley arrive to shut the operation down: the Circus withdraws its facilities, the cover arrangements and the diplomatic protection, and the Department is instructed to leave. It becomes plain that the Circus lent its help knowing what would happen, content to let a rival destroy itself with an operation the Circus never believed in. Leclerc, still talking about the Ministry and about the next stage of the operation, accepts the closure without appearing to understand it and prepares to report a success. Haldane, who expected nothing else, retreats behind his contempt. Avery, who promised Leiser that he would not be abandoned, breaks down. Leiser is left transmitting inside East Germany with no one listening and no way out, and the men who sent him fly home.
recaps.in_short: The Department, a British military intelligence organisation that has been decaying since the war, receives a report of Soviet missiles being moved near Kalkstadt in East Germany. Its Director, Leclerc, seizes on it as the operation that will restore the Department's standing. A courier, Taylor, is sent to Finland to collect film from an airline pilot and is killed on an icy road; the young aide sent to recover his effects, John Avery, bungles the trip completely. Undeterred, the Department revives its wartime methods and recruits Fred Leiser, a Polish agent it ran twenty years earlier and has not contacted since, now a garage owner in England. Trained in an Oxford house on obsolete wireless procedure and flattered into believing he is wanted, Leiser is sent across the border, killing a young sentry on the way. His transmissions are too slow and too long, and East German direction-finding locates him at once. At the last, Control and Smiley of the rival Circus close the operation down, having lent their help precisely so that the Department would ruin itself. Leiser is abandoned inside East Germany, and the men who sent him go home.

recaps.text: On a freezing northern airfield, Taylor, a courier for a British intelligence organisation known only as the Department, waits for a delayed flight. He is there to take delivery of a roll of film from Lansen, a civil airline pilot who has been paid to divert his route over a restricted area of East Germany and photograph what is on the ground. The handover is clumsy: Taylor has been drinking, the arrangements are amateurish, and the pilot is frightened and wants out. Carrying the film, Taylor walks out into the dark towards his hotel and is struck and killed by a car on the icy road. The film is not recovered. What was meant to be the Department's first real operation in years has cost a man's life in its opening hours and produced nothing.

In London the Department is revealed as a shabby remnant. Once a substantial wartime military intelligence organisation, it has shrunk to a few rooms, a dwindling staff and work nobody values, overshadowed by the better-funded civilian service, the Circus. Its Director, Leclerc, lives on memories of what the Department did in the war and treats the present crisis as its restoration. The cause of it all is a refugee report and a photograph suggesting Soviet rockets are being moved to Kalkstadt in East Germany, near the border. Around Leclerc are Haldane, the clever, ailing head of research, who despises the illusions but is drawn back into operational work, and Woodford, who is loud about the old days. Leclerc's young assistant John Avery, restless in an unhappy marriage and unsure what he is for, is delighted to be given his first real job: to fly north under a false name and recover Taylor's body and effects.

Avery's trip is a failure at every level. His cover name does not match his papers, the consul and the police are unhelpful, the hotel and the dead man's belongings are already picked over, and he finds nothing of the film. He is frightened, out of his depth and obliged to improvise lies he has not been taught to tell. The Circus, approached for help, provides it with a courtesy that costs it nothing. Avery comes home with the sense of having been tested and found wanting, and the Department greets him as a returning hero because it needs to. His wife Sarah, told nothing and asked to accept everything, is nearer to leaving him. Leclerc, so far from being deterred by two failures, concludes that the only remaining course is to put an agent on the ground inside East Germany.

Leclerc obtains Ministry approval and the Circus agrees, with unexpected readiness, to provide facilities. The Department goes to its wartime files and finds Fred Leiser, a Pole it ran as an agent twenty years ago, now naturalised, running a garage in the south of England and long forgotten by the service he risked his life for. Flattered by the approach and hungry to be one of them again, he agrees. He is installed in a rented house near Oxford and trained by Haldane, Avery and the old wireless instructor Johnson, using the procedures, codes and equipment of the last war because that is what the Department still knows. The set is heavy and slow, the schedules are inflexible, and none of it has been revised for twenty years of Soviet direction-finding. Avery, told to keep close to him, becomes genuinely attached, and lies to him steadily about how much the Department can protect him.

Training ends with Leiser fitter, better dressed and wholly convinced of his own importance, and with the men running him privately aware of how poor his chances are. Haldane says so; Leclerc does not listen. The party moves to Lübeck to set up a base station, and Leiser is taken to the border and put across at night. On the crossing he is challenged by a young East German frontier sentry and kills him with a knife, which shakes him badly and leaves a body that will be found. Inside, he makes his way towards Kalkstadt, stealing a motorcycle and living on nerve, and begins to transmit. The schedules are long, the procedure is obsolete, and he is on the air far past any safe limit. In Lübeck the operators take his signals, and the East German search for the source begins almost immediately.

Leiser reaches Kalkstadt, finds shelter with a young woman and continues to transmit at length from her room while the direction-finders converge. Whatever he has seen is never confirmed, and the Department's certainty about the missiles is never substantiated. At the base, Control and Smiley arrive from the Circus and end the operation: the facilities, the cover and the protection are withdrawn, and everyone is to go home. The Circus had assisted from the beginning in the expectation that the Department would destroy itself, and does not pretend otherwise. Leclerc, still speaking of the Ministry and the next phase, accepts the closure without appearing to understand what has happened to him. Haldane retreats into contempt. Avery, who promised Leiser that he would never be left, breaks down. Leiser goes on transmitting inside East Germany, hunted, with nobody listening and no way home, and the Department packs its equipment and leaves.
